rows.title: Manx shearwater
rows.evidence: The Manx shearwater article says the current English name refers to the nesting of this species on the Calf of Man, so the bird is named for this island.
rows.summary: The Manx shearwater was first described by Danish zoologist Morten Thrane Brünnich as Procellaria puffinus in 1764. The current scientific name Puffinus derives from "puffin" and its variants, such as poffin, pophyn, and puffing, which referred to the cured carcass of the fat nestling of the shearwater, a former delicacy. The original usage dates from at least 1337, but from as early as 1678, the term gradually came to be used for another seabird, the Atlantic puffin. The current English name was first recorded in 1835 and refers to the nesting of this species on the Calf of Man.

rows.title: Northern gannet
rows.evidence: The northern gannet article says the specific name bassanus is from the Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth, so the species is named for this island.
rows.summary: The specific name bassanus is from the Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth.

rows.title: Glanville fritillary
rows.evidence: The article says the Glanville fritillary is a highly restricted species within the UK, confined to the Isle of Wight, so the island is its principal UK stronghold. The following sentence notes the Channel Islands and an introduced site on the Hampshire coast.
rows.summary: The Glanville fritillary is a highly restricted species within the UK, being confined to the Isle of Wight and even there being largely limited to the southern coast. It also occurs in the Channel Islands, and since 1990 there has been a mainland site on the Hampshire coast, possibly the result of an introduction.

rows.title: Red-necked phalarope
rows.evidence: The Fetlar article says the Loch of Funzie is the most important breeding site in the United Kingdom for red-necked phalaropes, so Fetlar is the principal UK stronghold.
rows.summary: Of greatest importance are red-necked phalaropes, for which the Loch of Funzie is the most important breeding site in the United Kingdom, and for a while during the 1990s was the only breeding site in the country.

rows.title: Atlantic puffin
rows.evidence: The Isle of May article says the island is home to one of the largest puffin colonies in the United Kingdom, so the island is a principal stronghold.
rows.summary: The island is home to one of the largest puffin colonies in the United Kingdom.

rows.title: House mouse
rows.evidence: The Isle of May article says the island has its own unique race of house mice, so the race is endemic to this island.
rows.summary: The island also has its own unique race of house mice.

rows.title: European storm petrel
rows.evidence: The Mousa article says the island is designated as a Special Protection Area for storm-petrel breeding colonies and is known for storm-petrels, a principal stronghold.
rows.summary: The island is known for the Broch of Mousa, an Iron Age round tower, and is designated as a Special Protection Area for storm-petrel breeding colonies. Mousa is known for grey and common seals, black guillemots, Arctic terns and storm-petrels.

rows.title: Manx shearwater
rows.evidence: The Manx shearwater article names breeding colonies at Trollaval on Rùm, which is the atlas Isle of Rum.
rows.summary: The eerie, nocturnal cries of nesting shearwaters and petrels has led to associations with the supernatural. The breeding colonies at Trollaval on Rùm and Trøllanes and Trøllhøvdi in the Faroe Islands are believed to have acquired their troll associations from the night-time clamour.

rows.title: St Kilda house mouse
rows.evidence: The article says the St Kilda house mouse is an extinct subspecies found only on the St Kilda archipelago, and it names the St Kilda field mouse as a different subspecies that is still present. The house mouse is endemic to St Kilda and distinct from the field mouse already listed.
rows.summary: The St Kilda house mouse (Mus musculus muralis) is an extinct subspecies of the house mouse found only on the islands of the St Kilda archipelago of northwest Scotland. They were first described, alongside the St Kilda field mouse, by natural historian Gerald Edwin Hamilton Barrett-Hamilton in 1899. When the last St Kildans were evacuated in 1930, the endemic house mouse became extinct very quickly, as it was associated strictly with human settlement. The St Kilda field mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus hirtensis), a subspecies of the wood mouse, is still present.
